items.readable_text:
Content:
The vector projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto another vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is the portion that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] extends along [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
For example, consider two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] shown below. Suppose we know that [MATH: |\mathbf{a}|=2,] [MATH: |\mathbf{b}|=3,] and the angle between the vectors is [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/70c45a3fa72847dea43944c218fe8fcd]

Content:
The starting point of the vector projection is [MATH: O,] and the ending point will be the point [MATH: P] that lies on the line containing [MATH: \mathbf{b}] with [MATH: AP \perp \mathbf{b},] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c1f6a3e248a3fcd47b9077790ee3ebb8]

Content:
The vector [MATH: \overrightarrow{OP}] is called the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}.] It is denoted as [MATH: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},] and it is computed as

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= OP ⋅ u; = comp_{b}a ⋅ u]

Content:
where [MATH: \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta] is the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] and [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is a unit vector in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
First, we compute the scalar projection:

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 2\cos ((π)/(4)); = sqrt(2)]

Content:
Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}]

Content:
Therefore, the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= comp_{b}a ⋅ u; = sqrt(2) ⋅ (1)/(3)b; = (sqrt(2))/(3)b.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
When finding the projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b},] we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to [MATH: \mathbf{b}.] This happens when the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] extends in the direction opposite to that of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1a9f17a8c9a9ad3438b1098867c60a0f]

Content:
Consider two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b},] where it is known that
[MATH: |\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.]

Content:
Let's calculate [MATH: \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.]

Content:
First, notice that the angle between [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b] is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of [MATH: \mathbf b.]

Content:
Next, we compute the scalar projection:

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 2\cos (135^{∘}); = 2 ⋅ (− (sqrt(2))/(2)); = − sqrt(2)]

Content:
Notice that the scalar projection is negative.

Content:
Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}]

Content:
Therefore, the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= comp_{b}a ⋅ u; = − sqrt(2) ⋅ (1)/(3)b; = − (sqrt(2))/(3)b.]

Content:
This vector points in the direction opposite to [MATH: \mathbf{b},] as expected.

items.readable_text:
Content:
We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}]

Content:
However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|).]

Content:
Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting [MATH: \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},] we get

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|) ⋅ (b)/(|b|); = (a ⋅ b)/(|b|^{2})b; = (a ⋅ b)/(b ⋅ b)b.]

Content:
Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(b ⋅ b)b.]

Let [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\langle 1,-3,5 \rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}=\langle 5,-4,0 \rangle]. Find the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}].

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

[MATH: proj_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(b ⋅ b)b; = (a_{x}b_{x} + a_{y}b_{y} + a_{z}b_{z})/(b_{x}^{2} + b_{y}^{2} + b_{z}^{2})b; = (1 ⋅ 5 + (− 3) ⋅ (− 4) + 5 ⋅ 0)/(5^{2} + (− 4)^{2} + 0^{2})b; = (17)/(41)⟨5, − 4, 0⟩; = ⟨(85)/(41), − (68)/(41), 0⟩.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The vector projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto another vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is the portion that the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] extends along [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
For example, consider two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] shown below. Suppose we know that [MATH: |\mathbf{a}|=2,] [MATH: |\mathbf{b}|=3,] and the angle between the vectors is [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/70c45a3fa72847dea43944c218fe8fcd]

Content:
The starting point of the vector projection is [MATH: O,] and the ending point will be the point [MATH: P] that lies on the line containing [MATH: \mathbf{b}] with [MATH: AP \perp \mathbf{b},] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c1f6a3e248a3fcd47b9077790ee3ebb8]

Content:
The vector [MATH: \overrightarrow{OP}] is called the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}.] It is denoted as [MATH: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},] and it is computed as

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= OP ⋅ u; = comp_{b}a ⋅ u]

Content:
where [MATH: \text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta] is the scalar projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] and [MATH: \mathbf{u}] is a unit vector in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
First, we compute the scalar projection:

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 2\cos ((π)/(4)); = sqrt(2)]

Content:
Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}]

Content:
Therefore, the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= comp_{b}a ⋅ u; = sqrt(2) ⋅ (1)/(3)b; = (sqrt(2))/(3)b.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Direction of the Projection Vector

Content:
When finding the projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b},] we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to [MATH: \mathbf{b}.] This happens when the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] extends in the direction opposite to that of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1a9f17a8c9a9ad3438b1098867c60a0f]

Content:
Consider two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b},] where it is known that
[MATH: |\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.]

Content:
Let's calculate [MATH: \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.]

Content:
First, notice that the angle between [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b] is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of [MATH: \mathbf b.]

Content:
Next, we compute the scalar projection:

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 2\cos (135^{∘}); = 2 ⋅ (− (sqrt(2))/(2)); = − sqrt(2)]

Content:
Notice that the scalar projection is negative.

Content:
Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}]

Content:
Therefore, the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= comp_{b}a ⋅ u; = − sqrt(2) ⋅ (1)/(3)b; = − (sqrt(2))/(3)b.]

Content:
This vector points in the direction opposite to [MATH: \mathbf{b},] as expected.

---

Item 3 — Example: Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude

Example Prompt:
Suppose that [MATH: |\,\mathbf{a}\,|=8,|\,\mathbf{b}\,|=4] and that the angle between the vectors is [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}.] Find the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] in terms of the vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

[MATH: comp_{b}a|=|a|\cos θ; = 8\cos ((5π)/(6)); = 8 ⋅ (− (sqrt(3))/(2)); = − 4sqrt(3)]

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4} \mathbf{b}]

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

[MATH: proj_{b}a|= comp_{b}a ⋅ u; = − 4sqrt(3) ⋅ (1)/(4)b; = − sqrt(3)b]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: A General Formula

Content:
We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}]

Content:
However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

Content:
[MATH: comp_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|).]

Content:
Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting [MATH: \mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},] we get

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(|b|) ⋅ (b)/(|b|); = (a ⋅ b)/(|b|^{2})b; = (a ⋅ b)/(b ⋅ b)b.]

Content:
Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is

Content:
[MATH: proj_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(b ⋅ b)b.]

---

Item 7 — Example: Calculating a Vector Projection Using Components

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\langle 1,-3,5 \rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}=\langle 5,-4,0 \rangle]. Find the vector projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}].

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the formula for the vector projection, we obtain

[MATH: proj_{b}a|= (a ⋅ b)/(b ⋅ b)b; = (a_{x}b_{x} + a_{y}b_{y} + a_{z}b_{z})/(b_{x}^{2} + b_{y}^{2} + b_{z}^{2})b; = (1 ⋅ 5 + (− 3) ⋅ (− 4) + 5 ⋅ 0)/(5^{2} + (− 4)^{2} + 0^{2})b; = (17)/(41)⟨5, − 4, 0⟩; = ⟨(85)/(41), − (68)/(41), 0⟩.]

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: Projecting Perpendicular Vectors

Content:
Notice that if two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are perpendicular, then by projecting [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{b}] (or [MATH: \mathbf{b}] onto [MATH: \mathbf{a}]), we obtain the zero vector.

Content:
For example, the projection of [MATH: \mathbf{a}] onto a perpendicular vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] looks as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f3bb4c9d8854af35f141a1b60005492d]

Content:
Furthermore, we have the following fact:

Content:
> If [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.

---

Explanation:
